The Red-breasted meadowlark (Leistes militaris) begins life encapsulated within a calcareous egg that exhibits a mean length of 23.4 millimeters and a width of 17.2 millimeters. From these linear dimensions, the initial wet weight of the freshly laid egg can be reliably estimated at 2.6 grams [Ww0 = 2.6 grams], a modest starting mass for a bird of this body size. When incubated at a consistent temperature of 35 °C [T = 35 °C], the embryonated egg progresses through organogenesis over a period of approximately 14 days [ab = approximately 14 days] before the altricial nestling emerges. This incubation period is broadly comparable to that reported for other icterids of similar egg mass and reflects the rapid developmental pace enabled by sustained thermal conditions within the nest cup. Upon hatching, the first exogenous feeding occurs almost immediately as the nesting adult begins provisioning, initiating a phase of intense parental care.

During the nestling phase, the developing chick undergoes a striking transformation in body mass as the adult birds relentlessly deliver arthropod prey. Under the thermal regime of 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C], the fledgling stage is reached approximately 14 days after hatching [tx = approximately 14 days after hatching]. This relatively brief nestling duration is characteristic of many open-country passerines that face high predation pressure, necessitating rapid feather development and early departure from the nest. At the moment of fledging, the nestling’s attainment of flight feathers marks a critical transition from a fully dependent chick to a fledgling capable of short flights, though parental provisioning continues for some period thereafter as the young bird refines its foraging skills.

Sexual maturation in this species follows a predictable trajectory after the individual reaches nutritional independence. The attainment of puberty is recorded at approximately 42 days after hatching [tp = approximately 42 days after hatching] under the same sustained thermal condition of 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C]. This relatively early onset of gonadal maturation is notable among icterids and may be linked to their occupation of seasonally productive grasslands where breeding opportunities are temporally constrained. However, the first successful breeding event does not occur immediately upon reaching sexual maturity; instead, field records indicate that the time since birth at first brood averages 1.3 years since birth [tR = 1.3 years since birth] at 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C]. This considerable delay between physiological readiness and actual reproductive effort likely reflects the time required for young males to establish and defend territories and for females to accumulate sufficient body reserves for egg production.

Adult body mass exhibits pronounced sexual size dimorphism, a pattern common among polygynous icterids. Females attain an ultimate wet weight of 40.5 grams [Wwi = 40.5 grams], whereas males reach a substantially larger adult mass of 46.2 grams [Wwi = 46.2 grams], a difference of nearly 14 percent. This dimorphism is consistent with the species' lek-like mating system where larger males often enjoy greater success in aggressive encounters for display sites. The basal metabolic rate of this species, measured via respirometry at 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C], reaches a maximum of 79.5 milliliters of oxygen per hour [JOi = 79.5 milliliters of oxygen per hour], a value that falls within the expected range for a bird of this body mass when compared against allometric predictions for passeriformes inhabiting Neotropical savannas. The elevated resting metabolism likely supports the high levels of activity associated with aerial insectivory and sustained song production during the breeding season.

Longevity records for the Red-breasted meadowlark indicate a maximum lifespan of 10 years [am = 10 years] when maintained at 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C], a figure derived from field-based mark-recapture studies conducted across several populations in the Llanos ecoregion. This lifespan is moderately long for a passerine of its size and may reflect relatively low adult mortality in these productive grassland habitats compared to more arid regions. In terms of reproductive output, females typically produce 1 to 2 eggs per clutch [N_R_i = 1 to 2 eggs per clutch], with an average clutch frequency of approximately 1.3 clutches annually [F_R_i = approximately 1.3 clutches annually] under the thermal conditions of 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C]. This moderate fecundity is typical for tropical passerines that invest heavily in each nesting attempt through biparental care and extended post-fledging provisioning, thereby maximizing the survival prospects of a relatively small number of offspring across the breeding season.
